paras: The lynching of Oscar Coger was the hanging of a Black man by neighbors at Cherokee, Colbert County, Alabama, in late December 1887. Coger, accused of trying twice to set fire to the house of a widow, Mrs. Lindsay, was caught by men watching the house and hanged from a tree limb. A Montgomery Advertiser dispatch carried the story across the country, and a later local report said that men arrested for the lynching were released when no prosecutor appeared.

According to the Advertiser's special from Tuscumbia, someone entered Widow Lindsay's house at Cherokee one day in the last week of December, soaked the bed and carpet with kerosene and set them on fire. Mrs. Lindsay came home soon afterward, raised the alarm and saved the house with the help of friends or, in other versions, neighbors. One brief, carried in Waterbury and Freehold, New Jersey, described her as "a white widow"; the other reports did not give her race.

After the first fire the neighbors set a watch on the house, and they caught Oscar Coger, described as "colored," in what they said was a second attempt to burn it. They took him to a tree, which several versions placed a quarter of a mile away, and "swung him up to a limb." No account mentions an officer, a hearing or any statement by Coger.

The Advertiser reported that "the negroes here are indignant over the lynching" and that there was "considerable excitement," which shorter briefs rendered as "great excitement among negroes at Tuscumbia."

Near the end of January the Huntsville Gazette's correspondent for the Tuscumbia area wrote that "the parties supposed to have participated in the lynching at Cherokee were arrested," but were dismissed because no prosecutor appeared. Their names were not given, and no report of an inquest or indictment appears in the coverage.

The story spread from a single source, a special to the Montgomery Advertiser from Tuscumbia that was telegraphed out on January 2 and printed the next day in papers from Memphis and Savannah to Richmond and St. Paul. Headlines named Coger by the accusation: "A Fire Bug Lynched," "An Incendiary Lynched," "A Pyromaniae Lynched" and "An Incendiary Caught in the Act and Lynched." Weeklies kept the tone in later reprints, with Bismarck's "A Fire Bug Finished" and the Louisville Courier-Journal's "A Negro Fire-Bug ... Swung Into Eternity at a Rope's End."

News digests in Kentucky, Maine, Minnesota and elsewhere reduced the story to one line, some saying Coger was "hanged by a mob" for "alleged incendiarism" or "charged with incendiarism." These items repeated the wire's account of the capture without other sources, and only the Huntsville Gazette, in a local column, followed the case to the arrests.

The reports differ on the date: the Jan. 2 dispatch placed the capture in the previous week, while digests said Coger was lynched "on the 2d" or "on the 3d." Some briefs also put the lynching at Tuscumbia, the dateline town, rather than at Cherokee, where the wire placed the house.

reader.title: Lynching of Oscar Coger
bases: Neighbors who caught Oscar Coger, accused of trying to burn a widow's house, hanged him from a tree without any legal process (A2, A5), and digests called it hanging 'by a mob' (A15).

Coger was hanged from a limb by the neighbors who had watched the house, with no officer or court involved (A2, A5), a killing that other reports attribute to 'a mob' (A15); the stated reason was the alleged attempt to burn Mrs. Lindsay's house (A2, A15).

The Montgomery Advertiser's Tuscumbia special was widely reprinted (A2, A4, A5, A24), and a separate local item in the Huntsville Gazette independently refers to 'the lynching at Cherokee' and to arrests of supposed participants (A27).

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Advertiser special nearly verbatim under labels such as 'A Fire Bug Lynched', 'An Incendiary Lynched' and 'Lynching in Alabama', presenting the neighbors' capture of Coger in the act as fact.

The Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal's headline 'A Negro Fire-Bug ... Swung Into Eternity at a Rope's End' and the Bismarck 'A Fire Bug Finished' treated the hanging lightly and the guilt as settled.
Digest items gave one line, some marking the charge as 'alleged incendiarism'.

versions.value: Caught 'last week', before a Jan. 2 dispatch (late December 1887)

conflicts.note: The dated wire (A1, A2) is the primary source; the digest dates appear to be dispatch or publication dates, and the 3d postdates the Jan. 2 dispatch.
The wire places the house at Cherokee and was sent from Tuscumbia, Colbert County; the Tuscumbia versions appear to take the dateline for the scene.
